# Engine Oil Reducing to Half Without Leaks: Diagnosing Internal Consumption in Two-Stroke Engines

If you recently swapped engine oil on your Apache RTR 160 and noticed the level dropping from 1 liter back down to half within a short period, with no external leaks detected, you are dealing with internal consumption. This is a classic symptom of two-stroke engine wear, specifically related to piston ring dynamics and cylinder wall clearance. The Otul 5100 15W50 viscosity grade you selected is appropriate for high-temperature operation, but it does not prevent the mechanical reality that old engines consume lubricant as they age.

In a healthy two-stroke engine, oil mixes with fuel to lubricate the crankcase and cylinder walls before entering the combustion chamber. The piston rings act as the gatekeepers here. Their primary function is to seal the combustion pressure while scraping excess oil off the cylinder wall before it reaches the spark plug. When these rings wear down or become stuck due to carbon buildup, they lose their ability to scrape oil effectively. Consequently, the lubricant burns along with the gasoline, leading to significant consumption without any fluid escaping through seals or gaskets.

From a diagnostic standpoint, you must distinguish between external leakage and internal burning. Since you have ruled out leaks by inspecting the crankcase, chain guide, and cylinder head for wet spots, the focus shifts entirely to the combustion process. The most immediate indicator of this issue is fouled spark plugs. If you remove the plug and see heavy black soot deposits or oil sludge around the electrode, it confirms that oil is entering the exhaust port. This aligns perfectly with the symptoms of worn piston rings or cylinder wall scoring.

The trade-off here involves engine longevity versus immediate performance. Continuing to run an engine with half its required oil volume risks catastrophic failure if the consumption rate accelerates due to heat spikes. The lubrication film in the crankcase relies on a specific oil-to-fuel ratio; dropping below the minimum threshold can lead to increased friction and overheating of moving parts like the clutch basket and connecting rod bearings. While modern synthetic oils offer better thermal stability, they cannot compensate for a mechanical breach in the sealing system.

To address this technically, you need to inspect the piston rings and cylinder liner. If the cylinder walls are scored or the rings are broken, simply adding more oil will not resolve the underlying issue; it will only delay the inevitable seizure of the engine. In some cases, riders attempt to mitigate consumption by adjusting carburetor settings to reduce overall fuel flow, but this compromises power delivery and may cause lean-running conditions that damage the engine further. The correct engineering solution is often a mechanical overhaul or replacing the cylinder kit if the bore has been significantly enlarged beyond factory tolerances.

It is also worth noting that certain oil additives claiming to "seal rings" are generally ineffective on two-stroke engines because the combustion environment burns them away instantly before they can form a durable seal. The only reliable fix remains restoring the mechanical integrity of the sealing surfaces. If you operate your Apache in stop-and-go traffic or short-distance rides where the engine rarely reaches full operating temperature, carbon deposits can harden and stick to the rings, exacerbating the problem. Ensuring proper break-in procedures during future maintenance or switching to a slightly lower viscosity oil like 15W40 might help with cold starts, but it will not reverse the physical wear causing the rapid oil loss.
